newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Drought, lack of cash mar Kazakh '97 grain outlook.
newsitem.headline: Drought, lack of cash mar Kazakh '97 grain outlook.

text.p: Kazakhstan's 1997 grain harvest may fall to a net 13 million tonnes from an initially forecast 14 million tonnes due to drought and inadequate technology, a grain institute official said on Thursday.

"This year's grain harvest is likely to be 13 million tonnes, compared to the previous official forecast of 14 million tonnes," a department head at the ex-Soviet state's Grain Farming Research Institute said.

The official, who declined to be named, spoke from the institute's headquarters in the heart of Kazakhstan's nothern grain belt in the town of Shortandy, some 1,300 km northwest from the capital Almaty.

He said the institute, specialising in cultivating new types of grain and improving farming technologies, had revised its forecast for average grain yields this year to 0.7 tonnes per hectare or slightly more, from initial forecasts of 0.8 tonnes.
Some 17 million hectares were sown to grains this year.
The institute expects Kazakhstan to harvest around 10 million tonnes of wheat this year -- nearly the same amount as in 1996 but one million tonne less than forecast initially.
Last year's grain harvest -- hit by a severe drought -- totalled a meagre 11.6 million tonnes, or just a fraction of the over 20 million tonnes gathered annually in Soviet times.

"The main reason for revising this year's grain harvest is a drought," the official said. "But what also matters is that many cash-strapped farmers just cannot afford to observe all necessary technological operations."
He said a lack of funds on most farms delayed the beginning of spring sowing. Very little fertiliser was used.

"Most tractors and combine harvesters are 8-10 years old, and there is the usual lack of fuel...If all the technological operations had been applied, we could have counted on an additional 0.3-0.4 tonnes per hectare this year," he said.
Onal Shegebayev, director of the institute, said last month that poor use of fertilisers meant weeds took over up to 40 percent of Kazakhstan's grain harvest each year, pushing yields down.
Several southern regions have already started harvesting grains. Northern regions -- the producers of some 80 percent of Kazakh grain -- will start bringing crops in next week.
Despite stagnant production, Kazakhstan remains the largest exporter of grain in the Commonwealth of Independent States, with 4-5 million tonnes delivered abroad, mostly to Russia, a year.
Belarus and Azerbaijan are also large buyers of Kazakh grain.
